lines.text: A small land of mountain valleys that learned to stand apart from Europe's wars, and became home to the world's peacemakers. This is Switzerland.
Its story is traced to 1291, to a pact among the valleys of the Alps. Today it is a federation of cantons with four national languages.
That summer, the valleys of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden swore to stand by one another. The Swiss still call it their founding.
From that oath grew the Old Swiss Confederacy, a loose league of cantons that would win its freedom from the Habsburgs.
In 1315, at Morgarten, Swiss fighters ambushed a Habsburg army in a mountain pass, and beat it.
Two centuries later the priest Huldrych Zwingli brought the Reformation to Zurich, preaching from the Bible. He died fighting Catholic cantons.
In Geneva, the Frenchman John Calvin led reform of his own. His teaching spread to Scotland, the Netherlands and North America.
Geneva also gave the world Jean-Jacques Rousseau, whose Social Contract said that power comes from the people.
After Napoleon's invasion and fall, the powers meeting at Vienna in 1815 recognised Swiss neutrality. It has held ever since.
Henry Dunant, a Geneva businessman born in 1828, would found the Red Cross and share the first Nobel Peace Prize.
In 1848 a new constitution made Switzerland a federal state, with a parliament in Bern.
Rodolphe Lindt, born in 1855, would invent conching, the slow mixing that made Swiss chocolate smooth.
In 1863 Dunant and others founded the Red Cross in Geneva, to help the wounded, prisoners and civilians caught in war.
Two years later Edward Whymper's party first reached the top of the Matterhorn. On the way down a rope broke, and four men fell to their deaths.
In Vevey, Henri Nestle's infant cereal began a company that now sells coffee, chocolate and food around the world.
A young Albert Einstein worked in the patent office in Bern, where he wrote the papers that remade physics.
Le Corbusier, born in the Swiss Jura in 1887, would become one of the great architects of concrete and glass.
The International Olympic Committee was founded in 1894 and made Lausanne its home, one of many world bodies to settle in Switzerland.
FIFA, the body that runs world football, followed, and today it too is based in Zurich.
Rolex, founded in London, moved to Geneva in 1919 and became the best known name in luxury watches.
After the First World War, the League of Nations made Geneva its seat. It could not stop the wars of the thirties, but Geneva stayed a city of diplomacy.
In 1930 the Bank for International Settlements opened in Basel, the central bank for the world's central banks.
After the Second World War, which Switzerland stayed out of, Geneva became the second home of the United Nations.
The World Health Organization set up there in 1948, and went on to lead the campaign that ended smallpox.
In 1954 Switzerland hosted the World Cup, and in Bern, West Germany beat the mighty Hungarians in what is still called the Miracle of Bern.
That same year CERN was founded near Geneva. Its physicists would probe the smallest particles, and there the World Wide Web was born.
In 1971 the World Economic Forum began, and its yearly meeting in Davos now draws leaders from around the world.
The same year, Swiss men finally voted to give women the vote in federal elections, among the last in Europe to do so.
Roger Federer, born in Basel in 1981, would win twenty Grand Slam titles with a style that seemed effortless.
In 2008 CERN switched on the Large Hadron Collider, in a ring beneath the French border. Four years later it helped find the Higgs boson.
In 2016 the Gotthard Base Tunnel opened, about fifty-seven kilometres long, the longest railway tunnel in the world, straight through the Alps.
And in 2023, the banking country faced a shock, as the troubled Credit Suisse was rescued by its rival UBS.
From a pact of three valleys to the meeting place of the world, Switzerland's story goes on.
